The French looks passive, but your light bishop can be useful, and c5 and f6 are your key breaks.
notes.original:
1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5  Im sure that many of you have heard of the French Defence. The French Defence is a dynamic and solid defence against the move pawn to e4. It is also easy to play and doesn't really offer that much problem or challenges in the opening compared to the Sicilian Defence. Growing up Ive always hated the French Defence and I saw it as something that should not be played. Steinitz once said that the French Defence is the most dullest opening of all time. I agreed with that, I did not play the French Defence for a couple of reason. One is that the light square bishop is bad and it would ultimately be a big problem for black. Two it offers weaknesses on the kingside. Most of black's pieces usually aim at the queenside in which leaves the black king either in the center or castle. Problem is if black castles white can keep on attacking black until black surrenders. But the thing is I didn't know that the bad light square bishop can be of service despite of it being stuck behind the light
square pawn chain! First the light square bishop can be fianchettoed on b7. Black can also put the light square bishop on d7 followed by e8. Once f3 is played black can then proceed to put his light square bishop on h5! Things are different because of this! Black can also play Qb6 in the near future and exchange light square bishop with Bb5! Other alternatives include the a6 pawn push followed by Bb5! Now as for white's spacious advantage black can combat that with c5 and f3. They are the key important breakthroughs in the French Defence. Honestly I love the French Defence and it deserves a lot of respect.  *

notes.text: White avoids the French and plans a slow setup; the fight will be over the e-pawn.
notes.original:
It looks dubious for white from blacks perspective. This is probably best way to avoid French Defense positions. White plans to proceed with Nd2-Nf3-g3-Bg2-Qe2 setup.
Black has variety of moves how to proceed. Most of the battle will happen fighting for e pawn, be it on e4 or e5.

notes.original: A playable variation against the French Defence. But the problem in here is that this weakens the dark square diagonal on black's kingside with h7-g1. This also allows Ng6-Nf5. White cannot capture since the bishop is blocked by the f pawn. Furthermore this also slightly weakens white's kingside aswell.

notes.text: With pawns on c4 and e4, White's d-pawn lacks pawn support, which makes it a target.
notes.original: c4 the Steiner Variation weakens the d pawn. Because of white's weakening move of e4 and c4 the d pawn is effectively an isolated pawn.

notes.text: White can sidestep the classical French with Nf3, but it usually transposes after Nc3, so we follow that.
notes.original: This move could be played in order to avoid classical French. It can lead to exchange variation, but it is usually play with 3.Nc3. So we will focus only on that line here.

notes.text: An unusual surprise weapon that disrupts the usual French, though it is not thought as sound as d4.
notes.original:
An unconventional continuation. This disrupts the usual continuation of the French, so may be useful as an anti-theoretical surprise weapon, but it is not thought to be as sound as 2.d4.

If Black plays 2...d5 or 2...d6 (on turn two or later, e.g. 2...c5 3.Nf3 Nc6 4.c3 d6), White is ready to capture 3.exd6. White trades the e-pawn for the d-pawn, but unlike the exchange French (2.d4 d5 3.exd5 exd5) they avoid the drawish, symmetrical pawn structure.

Wilhelm Steinitz (1836―1900) debuted this opening in the 1882 Vienna tournament, where he played it six times including against Winawer (1838―1919), who played 2...f6. Though Steinitz played it occasionally for a short while afterwards (e.g. against Blackburne in 1883) it did not become his preferred line and he described it later as an "experiment".

In Die Französische Partie (German: The French Game) (1891), the first book of analysis dedicated to the French defence, Albert Heyde described it as (translating from German) "[having] the advantage of surprising the opponent, but it is significantly inferior theoretically to the usual continuation, 2.d4" and recommended the continuation 2...d5 anyway, allowing 3.d4 to transpose into an advance French or 3.exd6 e.p. Bxe6 4.d4 (4.Nf3 e5 5.d3 f5 6.Be2 Nf6 7.O-O O-O) 4...Nf6 5.Nf3 O-O.

It has not seen much serious tournament play since.

notes.text: Better is c5, striking at the centre.
notes.original: This strange move is the Chigorin Variation. If we play 2. ... d5 we just lose a pawn to 3. exd5 because our e-pawn is pinned. Better is 2. ... c5 (you can play that on the board)

notes.text: The French has drawbacks, like a hemmed-in light bishop and a weak e-pawn, but it is rich and dynamic.
notes.original: As a Caro Kann Player and an e4 player, I often frowned upon the French Defence and it isn't something of a good defence to meet the move e4. Why is that?Well my first reason is that the French Defence blockades the LSB (Light Square Bishop) which turns it into a horrible and passive bishop. Second reason is that black often has a weakness around his central pawn. A permanent weakness in which would ultimately may cause Black's downfall in the upcoming future. That is the e pawn. In most positions the e pawn often serves as a backward pawn in which would serve as a permanent weakness around Black's position. Third of all the French Defence gives white a spacious advantage with the advanced variation of the French Defence. White often gets an overextend central control in which may cause black challenges alongside White's attack on the kingside.Forth the French Defence's kingside is often attacked by White's forces. Since black often attacks and reinforces his pieces on the queenside white often attacks on the kingside. In many positions there is only a knight that can be quickly be of service to reinforce a complicated defence and a rook that was placed on the f8 square due to Black's castling manuever. But then there came a time when I switched my opening defence against e4 from Sicilian Defence to Caro Kann. The Sicilian Defence did brought me a fair amount of victories but It didn't really suited my style of playing chess. I prefer to lplay quiet games with little risk involved and a guaranteed safe investment amongst my vision and plan. I like to play Positionally instead of aggressive play. The Sicilian was heavy on theory and difficult to play because there are several moves and variations where black has to play a sequence of move in order to keep up with a good position.So I decided to switch to the Caro Kann Defence which I used to frown upon because the Caro Kann once again gives white a spacious advantage.I studied the Caro Kann for a long time and I thought for a moment "It isn't so bad after all! It's actually good!" Black does not have to worry about White's spacious advantage and initiative since it is often neutrelize because black is exhausting his effort in breaking up White's fortified central control!But then there came a time when I went with my family for a seven day vacation, roughly fifteen hours long trip! I brought my Loptop during this time and I have many PGNS and Chess Books that I can study alongside in my free time at the trip!After a long day of pleasure experience. I was tired and I didn't seemingly have the effort to read or to study chess via PGNS or PDFS. I began to crave for Chess Courses that was on video format. At first glimpse chessable was a great idea until you find out that you don't have an internet.So out of desperation I began to find any MP4, MOV, CBV, DVD etc. I was finding whether I have some video courses I left in my computer or hidden somewhere. With tough luck I remembered that I do not have any video courses downloaded because they take many spaces. I was unhappy and disappointed but then I found Simon William's "Killer French Defence DVD"At first sight It certainly wouldn't interest me since I don't like the French Defence. But then I began to take notice of it and finally caricatured "Fine I'll do it!"The DVD was old and I do not even remember where that DVD came from. But it certainly didn't disappoint me! I was educated how the French Defence works and my doubts and questions that hindered me from being in favoured of the French Defence was suddenly changed. The French Defence is beautiful!It changed my perspective towards the French Defence. I usually get bored when it comes to watching Video courses. There are many Chessable courses that really bore me but I won't mention them. Regardless whether I spent tens of hours on that particular course it actually didn't even bore me! I was even fascinated and filled with joy!I learned that the French Defence is a beautiful Positional and Dynamic Defence. It's a good opening choice to meet e4 and regardless whether black may have certain challenges in the opening. They can be fixable and a resolution is often profound. I was happy learning the French Defence. To express my gratitude and joy I'll be teaching you how to play it! PS: I'll tip GM Simon William's also known as GingerGM handsomely on this one!"

notes.text: The French Defence is on the board; a little practice will help you master it.
notes.original: The French Defence on the board! It would only take a couple of times before you master the French Defence!

notes.text: The French Defence is one of the oldest and most played defences against White.
notes.original: The French Defence on the board! One of the oldest and most played defence against white!

notes.text: If White advances e5, you hit d4 with c5, Nc6 and Qb6 to undermine White's centre.
notes.original: In the advance variation of the French Defense, White counters the threat to the e4 pawn by advancing the pawn, creating a space advantage with locked pawn chains in the center. The main line of the Advance Variation continues 3... c5 4. c3 Nc6 5. Nf3 and then we have a branching point: 5... Qb6, the idea is to increase the pressure on d4 and eventually undermine the white centre. The queen also attacks the b2-square, so White's dark-square bishop cannot easily defend the d4-pawn without losing the b2-pawn. White's most common replies are 6.a3, 6.Be2 and 6.Bd3.

notes.text: The Exchange Variation is White's simplest try against the French, perhaps aiming for an improvised London setup.
notes.original: The French Defence: Exchange Variationis the easiest way white can play against the French Defence. There are two reason why white is playing the French Defence. First and foremost white maybe doesn't know much about theory, so he decided to exchange pawns to keep things simple. Second reason is that white is going to settle for the Improvised London System against the French Defence.

notes.text: White gains space, but you strike back at the center with your c-pawn and f-pawn.
notes.original: Perhaps it is a little too early to talk about the Advance Variation of the French Defence. But believe me when I say the Advanced Variation of the French Defence is the most challenging way to play against. Let's examine the position.-White gets a spacious advantage-White can launch a potential attack on the kingside since black usually doesn't have that much defender around the kingside. -White can cause complications on the kingside with early Queen moves.-If White was able to hold unto his central pawn black would certainly crumble!-Last but not least, Black's one of biggest problem, the LSB. Certainly White does get a lot of PROS in here. But that does not mean white gets an easy play in here! Black would attack white's central control right away. Since white's center is loose and not fortified white often does not hold on to his spacious advantage. White is free to relinquish his spacious advantage. But that only comes if black does not do anything.Black's major breakthrough in here is the f pawn and the c pawn. The e pawn is often the remain of White's advanced pawn formation.

notes.text: The Advance is White's most challenging try against the French.
notes.original: The Advanced French Defence, the most challenging and the best response for white if white wants to withhold tensions.

notes.text: In the Advance Variation you aim to break up White's center while White tries to hold it.
notes.original: The Advanced Variation of the French Defence. This is the most challenging French Defence variation ever. Black's goal is to breakup White's center whereas white would try and fortify the center.

notes.text: White gains space with e5, but the game is about to get messy.
notes.original: As usual white should advance his pawn forward gaining a spacious advantaage, but in exchange white should be wary and be on the lookout of what he is entering, for things are about to be messy in this particular game.

notes.text: The Classical French is the most common, flexible reply, and less testing for you than the Advance.
notes.original: The classical French Defence. Usually the most common opening variation against the French Defence since this is very flexible and easy to play. Black may face some certain challenges when it comes to this position. But eventually the Classical is less challenging than the Advance French Defence.

notes.text: Nc3 is the most common move: White develops and keeps the central tension, leaving you many options.
notes.original: The Classical Variation This is the move that is often played in the French Defence.White develops his knight and keeps the tension on the center. Black has many options in here. One of them is Nf6!? And Bb4! All of which are highly theoretical. Although the Winawer variation and the usual Nf6!? Are covered in this French Defence in this course. On a brief meantime let me introduce you to my number one recommendation in the Classical French.

notes.text: The Exchange Variation gives a symmetrical, quiet structure that is often drawish, and it was once the main French line.
notes.original: This is the Exchange Variation of the French Defence. Up until the mid-19th century this was regarded as the main line of the French Defence. The Exchange Variation is a dull, drawish, and static opening, prompting Wilhelm Steinitz to write, "I have never in my life played the French Defense, which is among the dullest of openings." It was only around the 1860s and 1870s that the variations arising after 3.Nc3, 3.Nd2, and 3.e5 became popular.The Exchange Variation leads to a symmetrical pawn structure. Both sides often develop symmetrically, while giving no room for imbalance in the game, which is why the opening is so drawish. Players who want a draw only will often employ the Exchange Variation.

notes.text: Nd2 stops your Winawer pin; just trade pawns on e4 and keep things simple.
notes.original: The move Nd2 prevents Black from entering the Winawer (3.Nc3 Bb4). The knight on d2 exerts no pressure on d5 and may lead to slower development of white's pieces but the move is solid and leads to games of a more positional nature than its main alternative of 3.Nc3. In here however I wouldn't recommend playing Nc6!? e5! Would have been a long struggle for black. Instead just exchange pawns and keep things simple. The Rubinstein variation is similar to the Karpov Variation of the Caro Kann and it also doesn't really deal with chaotic and complications in the opening itself.

notes.text: In the Perseus Gambit White gives a pawn and plans Ne5 to pressure your f7 pawn.
notes.original: The Perseus Gambit White is sacrificing a pawn for little compensation. White is going to play Ne5 to try and as much as possible to pressurize the f7 pawn and so on. There are a few traps that may arose from this position.

notes.text: This is rare and mostly seen in blitz; you can equalise, but play actively with dxe4, c5 or Bb4.
notes.original:
Not often played for white, it usually appears in blitz games.
Black can equalize position early in the game, though white has tricky counterplay. Black has to be aggressive in his intentions.
Common continuations for black :
1.) dxe4 ; Most natural, forcing white to take on e4 and developing Nf6 soon. White stays with strong LSB while black is not behind on development.
2.) c5 ; Agressive hit in the center. It can get in simmilar position as exchange variation with isolated d pawn.
Keeps possibility of transposing to advanced variation.
3.) Bb4+ ; seems dubious, but is actually quite frequently played. Some people say it is one of the best moves here as it forces white to play c3 and stop from natural development of queenside. Simmilar to advanced variation.

notes.text: Your c-pawn hits d4, fighting back against White's advanced center instead of being suffocated.
notes.original: The best response against the Advance Variation. Black needs to fight back against White's central pawn or otherwise suffocate!

notes.text: Striking back with c5 is almost forced, hitting White's pawn center right away.
notes.original: Eventually, there's really not much of a good option other than the move c5 immediately striking back towards white's expansion towards the center.

notes.text: The c5 break is your key idea, striking at the d4 pawn.
notes.original: Black's key point is the move c5. Energetic breakthrough. Black will then have to deal with his bad bishop by swapping it of after the move a6.

notes.text: Your f6 challenges the center at once, but it weakens your light squares; g6 can patch them.
notes.original: This is my favorite one, black immediately challenges white's less fortrified center right away with the move f3?! It is not advicable to play the move f3 if black hasn't castled or developed his pieces. Black creates an immediate weakness on the kingside and that is the light squares. Black's king is very vulnerable! But seriously why do I still like the move f3?! Well as a matter of fact since white hasn't developed any of his pieces yet theres no immediate attack on the kingside. The light square weaknesses can easily be patched with the move g6. Black will keep attacking white's center whereas white has to defend. Black also dreams of an open f file once black castles. Once the f file is open and the dark square bishop lands on c5 black has a very good attack against white. Problem in here is that white can constantly attack black as of then since black isn't really doing that much which postpones or discourages white's constant attack.

notes.text: White's c3 pawn supports the center by guarding the d4 pawn.
notes.original: As usual there are couple of alternatives in here such as Nc3. But c3 is the most favoured move in here. The move c3 supports the center.

notes.text: The c3 pawn backs up d4, but White's central pawns are overextended.
notes.original: Another alternative in which eventually supports White's overexpansion towards the central pawns.

notes.text: c3 is one of White's best replies, holding up the overextended d4 pawn.
notes.original: One of White's finest attempt and strongest reply in here. Trying to keep up with the overextended pawns.

notes.text: White's c3 props up the d4 pawn and opens the queen's diagonal toward a4.
notes.original: The usual response in this particular opening is the move c3 in which stabilises white's central pawns and also opens up the d1-a4 diagonal.

notes.text: Nc3 develops, but with the c-file closed there is no Winawer, so you must free your light bishop.
notes.original: Developing the knight, eventually since the Winawer French could no longer be achieved in here since the c file is already closed. Black has to make ways in getting the light square bishop off.

notes.text: Bb5 check is fine for White; equality is expected, and trading bishops rids you of your bad bishop.
notes.original: Bb5 check Is frankly not a bad move. But total equality is what both opposing side should expect. The exchange of bishops would simplify the position and is much easier to play. Since white has played Bb5 white is obligated to either take the light square bishop thus Black's problem with the bad bishop is gone. Or retreat back the bishop in which loses a tempo.

notes.text: Bd3 is a quiet choice that leaves equality and gives you few problems.
notes.original: White is just looking forward for a nice game of chess and total equality is made in here. Eventually white did not aim for variations in which gives black much challenges other than the move Bd3.

notes.text: White wasted time and gave up its centre; develop your knight, since e5 and c5 are weak.
notes.original: "Why don't you wake up your your knight, ." "White intends Bc1-e3." "What about Nb8-c6, ? first of all the e5 pawn is very weak and the c pawn is also hanging." I frankly do believe that this is a mistake for white. White basically just wasted a tempo building up his center only to give it all away in the near future.

notes.text: White gives up the center too easily; your c5 pawn can simply take on d4.
notes.original: Whats the point of playing the Advance French Defence if you are going to let go of your central pawns easily and right away? White must be oblivious to do so!

notes.text: Develop your knight to c6, adding pressure on the d4 pawn.
notes.original: "You should really play Nc6, " "The silicon chessplayer would appear to be threatening Ng1-f3"

notes.text: Nc6 is the usual main line; develop your bishop to d7 and knight to e7 next.
notes.original: Nc6 is the usual main line in here. Although other alternative such as Bd7 is frankly possible. But I prefer Nc6 first followed by Bd7 Ne7 and so on.

notes.text: Your plan is Qb6 and then Bb5, trading your bad light bishop for White's good one.
notes.original: Black's idea in here is to play Qb6 followed by Bb5 to exchange the bad light square bishop to white's good light square bishop.

notes.text: Your c5 and f6 pawns challenge White's centre on both wings, so White can't attack quickly.
notes.original: f3 was made possible in here because white played the move c3 thus the move Bd3 is delayed. Unlike the move f3?! right away after e5! Things would have gotten a bit cranky after the move Bd3. c5 followed by f6 is better since black challenges white's center right away with the move c5 thus forcing white to react right away with the move c3 (Other alternatives are not as strong as the move c3) Since black challenges both white's center on the queenside and the kingside. White would not be able to attack right away since black has some tactical sequences which would be able to counterattack white's attack.

notes.text: Rare idea: Bd7, take on d4, then Bb5 to swap bishops, at the cost of your queenside structure.
notes.original: This has fallen out of favour and only seen a few times. The idea in here is to play Bd7 followed by pawn takes pawn then Bb5! Exchanging the light square bishop to white's! However many do not like this because first of all the b pawn is doubled and the queenside pawn structure is damaged. Black do get some compensation due to the fact that black has a semi opened a file.

notes.text: A fun sideline: b6 and Ba6 swap your bad light bishop for White's good one, though it's dubious.
notes.original: A fun sideline in which black plays Ba6 to exchange his bad light square bishop into white's strong and good light square bishop. Although this is a bit dubious due to the fact that black isn't aiming to break up white's center in blitz. It is still a fun sideline to surprise your opponent.

notes.text: Nf3 is the main line: White simply develops a piece and builds from there.
notes.original: Nf3 is the main line in here. Nf3 simply developing a piece and further progress can be made out of piece development and activity in here.

notes.text: Bb5 is common at club level but weak: White must trade for your knight or lose time retreating.
notes.original: Bb5 is often common amongst Club Players. I do believe that Bb5 is not White's strongest move in here since it doesn't bare any challenges to black. Its a waste of move and white is often obligated to take the knight for the bishop or otherwise retreat back the bishop and lose a tempo.

notes.text: White's f4 only pays off once you castle kingside; for now you have little to worry about.
notes.original: f4 is only beneficial once black has castled kingside. Eventually white is aiming for a Dutch Defence or Bird Opening idea where an immediate attack on the kingside can be made once black castles. Black really has nothing much to worry about in here other than castling.

notes.text: White's light bishop is hemmed in by your light-square pawns, so White may reroute it toward the kingside.
notes.original: The Light Squared Bishop is a bad bishop in here since it is blockaded by Black's light square pawn chain. An usual idea in here is to manuever the bishop to White's kingside from e1 to h5.

notes.text: Your queen supports the c5 pawn break and looks toward the g2 pawn.
notes.original: Qb6 eyeing on the g2 pawn and at the same time support the c5 pawn breakthrough.

notes.text: White's a3 prepares b4 to challenge your c5 pawn, which makes castling long harder for you.
notes.original:
Might not be the best continuation for white, but it is getting more and more popular. 6.a3 is a move which challenges c5 pawn with b4.
Black has pretty much the same plan here; opening c or f file and trying to destroy white"s center. The main difference is that black will have harder time going into O-O-O as white could be really fast with b4 break on the queenside.

notes.text: White wants to fianchetto its blocked light bishop, which is a respectable idea.
notes.original: Eventually white wants to fianchetto his light square bishop since it is blockaded with the knight. I do believe that this move is respectable.

notes.text: Your c4 advance only works once White's queenside pawns have moved, as here.
notes.original: c4 is possible once the move b3 was eventually played. Keep in mind that the advance of pawns to c4 is not possible if White's a or b pawn is still complete.

notes.text: Your knight heads for f5, where it will press on the d4 pawn.
Your knight is headed for b3, and White's knight is tied to guarding that square.
notes.original: Nb3 is the plan in here, Black's knight is ready to put his knight towards the b3 square. White's knight is stuck defending the b3 square.

notes.text: Your queen eyes the e5 pawn and clears the back rank for castling long.
Your h-pawn keeps White's pieces out of g5 and backs your g-pawn's advance.
Your knight reaches b3 because White's knight left, and it was the only guard of that square.
notes.original: Nb3 was made possible since White's knight moved away. The only piece defending the b3 square.

notes.text: Your bishop gets outside its own pawns and backs up the knight on b3.
Your g-pawn kicks the bishop off f4 and grabs space on the kingside.
Your knight lands on f5, hitting the d4 pawn and White's bishop on g3.
Your king tucks behind the locked queenside, freeing your kingside pawns to advance.
You take back the knight, and your f-pawn can now advance to hem in White's bishop.
Your f-pawn chases the bishop to h2, where it is shut in behind your pawns.
Your king slides to a safer square and guards the a7 pawn.
Your knight steps aside so your bishop hits White's queen, and it eyes d3 next.
Your knight blocks the e5 pawn, guards your f4 pawn and hits d4.
This line scores 65% for Black, and 64% if White takes on c6.
notes.original: Overall 65% Winrate for Black, 64% if White takes on c6.

notes.text: You trade queens, and White's bishop has to leave b5 to take back.
Trading queens suits you, and you are heading for an endgame.
notes.original: The exchange of queens would do we for black. Black is headed for an endgame in here.

notes.text: Your bishop breaks the pin, so your knight is free to take the e5 pawn.
Your knight takes safely: moving it uncovers your bishop's attack on White's loose bishop.
Recapturing with the knight also attacks White's unguarded c5 pawn.
Your queen pins the c3 pawn to White's king, so it cannot take back.
You grab the bishop; if the pawn takes your queen, your knight takes White's.
You win the queen back, keeping both bishops against White's doubled b-pawns.
You are doing better: your bishop pair gives you the initiative.
notes.original: Black is eventually doing better in here! Black has the initiative since be has the bishop pair.

notes.text: Your pawn takes back toward the centre and gives d5 extra support.
Your queen takes the pawn back and eyes f2 from an active square.
Your knight is on its way to f5, an active square near White's centre.
Your shut-in bishop finds an open diagonal and hits the rook on f1.
Your knight takes its active post and frees e7 for your bishop, then you castle.
Your last minor piece is out, and you are ready to castle next.
Your queen steps away from the knight's attack and backs the c-pawn's advance to c5.
Your c-pawn takes the d4 square away from White's knights and gains central space.
White's g4 looks dubious, since it weakens White's own kingside.
notes.original: Perhaps a bit dubious in here. Why is white willing to play g4 thus weakening his kingside?

notes.text: Your knight dodges the pawn and offers a trade that drags White's knight to the rim.
Your pawn forks White's bishop and knight, so you get your piece back.
The comment warns that White's next pawn push leaves your bishop on h4 trapped.
notes.original: Bxh4 is just not possible because of h5! The bishop is now trapped!

notes.text: Your knight joins the c-pawn in attacking d4, which only White's queen defends.
Bb5 is a wasted move: White must trade for your knight or retreat and lose a tempo.
notes.original: I do believe that the move Bb5 is a mistake here, in the French Defence Advance Variation the Light Square Bishop is useful since white's pawn is placed on the dark square. Swapping off bishops would only weaken the light squares. But considering that Bb5 is played it is frankly a waste of move since white has to exchange bishop for knight or otherwise retreat back the bishop thus losing a tempo.

notes.text: You take the d4 pawn, and your new pawn attacks White's knight on c3.
You may keep the extra pawn, but White's knight gets strong counterplay with the d6 square.
notes.original: Black may have the chance to keep this pawn in the near future but in exchange white has a strong counterplay since the d6 square is entitled for White's knight.

notes.text: Your bishop guards the extra d4 pawn and covers d6 against White's knight.
White plans b4 for a queenside minority attack, and the knight wants d6.
notes.original: White is planning to play b4! With a minority attack on the queenside and at the same time the d6 square is available for White's knight to take advantage of.

notes.text: Your knight on c6 attacks the knight on d4, so this capture doesn't work for White.
notes.original: Not possible since the d pawn us going to be taken away by Black's knight.

notes.text: Your knight on c6 hits the new knight on d4.
notes.original: Not possible since the d pawn would be taken by black's knight.

notes.text: Your knight develops toward g6, where it will attack the e5 pawn.

notes.original: An interesting gambit to meet the French Defence. White's goal is to play Bc4 and have a quick attack on the kingside. FM Dennis Monokroussos described the Latvian Gambit as “possibly the worst opening in chess.” If he is correct, then the Orthoschnapp Gambit must surely come a close second. The Orthoschnapp Gambit is played against the French Defense. Yes, white gets some attacking chances by creating a queen and bishop battery aimed at f7, but this is not enough compensation for the pawn against the correct defense.The Orthoschnapp Gambit is worth trying in blitz or bullet chess because you only give up a pawn. Honestly I'm surprised that from all of the French Defence DVD, courses, books, and so on the Orthoschnapp Gambit was never mentioned.

notes.original: 5.Bc4 can get met with 5…Qe7, but …Qd7 makes it easier for black to castle. In this variation, black gives back the material to obtain the bishop pair and a lead in development. The open lines will make the bishops particularly powerful as they take aim at the white kingside. Black will also get pleasant control of the d-file after long castle with the rook supporting the queen. Objectively the black position might only be slightly better, but it is undoubtedly more straightforward and more pleasant to play. Remember, playing positions you are comfortable in is more important than the chess engine evaluation of the position. Unless you are playing one of the world’s elite, a 0.1 or 0.2 change in the assessment is unlikely to make a difference to the game’s result.

notes.original:
The Orthoschnapp Gambit is a testament to how tough the French Defense can be challenging to meet. There is no greater compliment to a defense than forcing the other side to contemplate playing unsound gambits. For those gambit players still in search of a gambit to play against the French Defense, the Wing Gambit, which you can also use against the Sicilian Defense, or Milner-Barry Gambit, are excellent options. Players who prefer not to enter the tactical world of gambits could find the Tarrasch Variation more to their liking. The Orthoschnapp Gambit is not suitable for beginners. The French Defense is a tough defense to win against, and if you are a beginner looking for a way to play against the French Defense, you could try the Wing Gambit or 1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.Bd3. GM Simon Williams, who often plays the French Defense, has called the Wing Gambit a dangerous weapon for white. Credits belongs to Shaun Sedice: His Chessable blog on the Orthoschnapp Gambit

notes.text: A crossroads, and f6 is best: it hits White's e5 pawn and opens the f-file.
notes.original:
This are the crossroads. Now black decides what to do. Good possibilites are :
7. .. f6 ; In my opinion best move in this position. It destroys whites solid center and opens f file. Also white is pretty much forced to exchange exf6 and release tension on f6 and d6 squares. It also keeps isolated d pawn in center which can be huge target in the game. I will cover this line first.
7. .. Qb6 ; Solid move. It puts more pressure on whites d pawn and b2 pawn and it forces white to go Nf3. Problem with this Qb6 is that Nd7-Bd7 will be stuck there for a while, so f6 will have to be played sooner or later. That is why I think f6 is much better option because it does not waste a move on pretty simmilar position you get with immediate f6, but you have already taken a potential square for Nb6 and Bd7. Also in 7. .. f6 variation, Queen goes on c7 to refute DSB exchange on f4 and putting strong Nf4.
7. .. Nb6 ; Decent move. It develops piece on active square and it is aiming toward c4. This move shows early signs that black will play more on queenside and most likely will not be playing f6 anytime soon or if ever. It also enables Bd7 and Be7 with O-O early.
7. .. Be7 ; Passive move, but playable. I avoid it as white LSB becomes very active and playing O-O can put you under imminent attack after f4 and Nf3 setup.
7. .. f5 ; Not very much played move, but GMs used to play it. I personally dont like it as it keeps weak e6 pawn for whole game. Pros are that LSB comes pretty much useless as it is hitting in the pawn. This can be very aggressive. Black usually goes for Be7, O-O, h6 and g5. It keeps semi open position on kingside and it can be very sharp.

notes.original: This is very interesting variation to play. Seems like black is losing a pawn, while actually black will sacrifice material for initiative.

notes.text: Your queen backs the d6 bishop, stopping a bishop trade and keeping the diagonal toward h2 under pressure.
notes.original: Very important move for black. It keeps white from trading off DSBs and keeps pressure on h2 pawn and whole kings side along with d6-h2 diagonal.

notes.text: Your rook eyes the f3 knight, so Rxf3 is a constant tactical threat.
notes.original:
Black has many tactics here. Rxf3 is constant threat which in certain positions can lead to whites collapse of the position.
White could press kings side with simple plan such as Bb1 and Qc2 ( Qd3 ). Forcing black to weaken his kings side with g6.

notes.text: White's queen had to come out; a bishop to b4 would pin the d2 knight.
notes.original: As long as queen remains on the back rank, white cannot move his Nd2 anywhere, because Bb4 is a serious threat. Qh4 is forced.

notes.text: You're down a rook for a knight, but your center, safe king and White's doubled f-pawns compensate.
notes.original: Black is down with material ( Rook for a knight) but position is actually very good. Very active, full center, king is safe, can overtake c file soon, no weak LSB which was traded for whites good LSB, and open f8-b4 file, white pawn structure is prety weak with doubled f pawns.

notes.text: This shows how quickly White collapses without precise play; your bishop now attacks the b2 rook.
notes.original: Last few moves were example if white does not play precise, position can collapse very soon.

notes.text: Your counterplay aims at g2 down the g-file, or you can push c5.
notes.original:
This is tipical setup one gets in this variation. Black will play through g file or through pushing c5. e5 might also be possible. g2 is the main square where black will find his counterplay.
White will pursue c4 will full center. Pushing a pawn or simply pressing the already pinned Nf6 with Nf4->Nh5 and winning e pawn back.

notes.text: Typically you play knight e7, castle and then f6, while White eyes a4 and Ba3.
notes.original:
Not very popular for white, but certainly playable. White has a plan to keep the strong center and to make use of blacks lack of DSB by playing a4 and Ba3.
Black has to be carefull here. Tipically it goes with Nge7, O-O and f6.

notes.text: White can grab the g7 pawn with the queen.
notes.original:
White has to make decision. Either going Qxg7 or playing Nf3. Both options are good. Most of the time when white plays 4. e5 , he/she is trying to prevent those very aggressive moves like Qxg7.
The key difference is that white is not gambiting e pawn, so pressure on d6 and f6 remains the same, especially as there is no DSB.

notes.text: Or White can simply develop the knight to f3; both options are good.
notes.original:
White has to make decision. Either going Qxg7 or playing Nf3. Both options are good. Most of the time when white plays 4. e5 , he/she is trying to prevent those very aggressive moves like Qxg7.
The key difference is that white is not gambiting e pawn, so pressure on d6 and f6 remains the same, especially as there is no DSB.

notes.text: You must castle now, then develop your light bishop and open the f-file.
notes.original: Move which avoids sharp positions like in the main line. Now black has to castle. White will go on development. Black has chronically weak LSB, so developing this piece and openng f file is a must.

notes.text: Aim your rooks at White's king along the open g and h files, and push your d-pawn.
notes.original:
Tipical position you get in this types of french. Now game is on, everything can go upside down.
White will try to keep material and develop last pieces. a4-Ba3 is a known setup here too.
Black will play to attack king in the center over open h and g file and pushing d4.

notes.text: A very common French sacrifice: you give a rook for initiative and active pieces.
notes.original: Very common material sacrifice in French defense. It is everything about initiative and piece placement in such games.

notes.text: You are down material, but your position is better.
notes.original: Black is down on material, but better.

notes.text: A drawish position; to win it you must exploit White's doubled c-pawns and weak a-pawn.
notes.original: Not position I would love to play with either white or black. Very drawish, so I tend to avoid it. To win this position, you need to have high understanding of positional game to be able to exploit whites not so good pawn structure.

notes.text: You are in trouble: White's bishop presses on d6 and Qg4 is coming, so you must give material back.
notes.original: Black has a lot of trouble. White gave pawn away for a valuable initiative and pressure on d6 square. Qg4 will be next move or Bd6. Depending on black, but black has to give material back.

notes.text: This is the only move that holds: it stops White's b5, which would cramp your queenside.
notes.original: From my experience as white player against French, this is the only move which actually holds position. If white can play b5 it will pressure blacks queenside and development will be next to impossible for black.

notes.text: A precise move: it defends the d4 pawn and prepares b4 sooner.
notes.original: This is the most precise move here in my opinion. White defends d pawn and also it makes possiblity to play b4 sooner. Be3 is slower move. DSB should go to f4 or keep it at c1 square for some time.

notes.text: Be aggressive: prepare queenside castling and Bd6 to attack where White does not expect it.
notes.original:
You have to be aggressive in this sort of positions. If white prepared exchange variation, he definetely did not expect attacking on queenside.
So black is preparing O-O-O with Bd6.

notes.text: White is stuck: rooks and bishops are badly placed and the queenside attack is far off.
notes.original: Now, if you look at the position, white is kind of stuck. Rooks on wrong places, bishops on wrong places, queenside attack is not even near to start. White can easily get lost in this sort of positions.

notes.text: You are faster on the kingside; f6 and g5 matter most, but it is not yet won.
notes.original:
Black is simply faster. Ng8 should stay there for some time, there is norush in developing. Key move here is f6. Blocking e5 square and pushing g5 is by far more important.
Black is simply faster on the kingside attack.
It is still not won game, however, black has great counter play.
This was just a sort of manual how to engage aggressively on exchange variation of French defense. White players usually do not understand it and even less expect it.

notes.text: Your bishop shields your king on the open e-file and clears the way to castle.
Your king leaves the open e-file before White can line up a rook on it.
Your knight leans on the d4 pawn and makes taking on c4 a real idea.
Your bishop pins the knight that guards d4, so that pawn feels the strain.
You have two main choices: dxc4 for a sharp, double-edged fight, or Nb4 to isolate White's d4 pawn.
notes.original:
This is the most common position to get. Black has few choices now.
1.) dxc4; which complicates the position the most. Winning d pawn, but also losing b7 pawn. Now, this gives great tactical potential for both sides, so it is double edged sword.
2.) Nb4; it forces white to either recapture on d5, isolating white d4 pawn and retreating his LSB to e2.

notes.text: Your knight chases the d3 bishop, so taking on c4 next will isolate d4.
Taking on c4 leaves White's d4 pawn isolated, with no pawn beside it to help.
Your plan is easy: queen to d7, then c6, and a rook to d8, with White slightly worse.
notes.original:
This is position I prefer. It is usually best way for black. Building tension on d pawn.
Now black has easy plan, Qd7-c6-Rad8 setup. White is in weaker position.

notes.text: White is better developed and your bishop and rooks are passive; Nb4 on move nine keeps you calmer.
notes.original:
Not my cup of tea. White got tactical advantage and better developed pieces. Blacks DSB is in a bit passive position and rooks are on their passive position as well.
Position is playable for both sides, but I would highly recommend 9. ... Nb4 as it keeps black in calm and better position with white standing passive.

notes.text: Your bishop backs up the d5 pawn, which White's c-pawn and knight both attack.
Your knight takes the pawn back and piles onto White's pinned knight on c3.
Your knight comes out attacking the d4 pawn, which nothing defends right now.
Your king gets safe, and the rook is ready to take the open e-file.
Now develop your queenside knight.
notes.original: And, let's develop our b8-knight.

notes.text: Qe2 invites an exchange on e4, but that allows a check on b5; White's bishop still reaches g2.
notes.original:
White often time tries to avoid exchange on d5. That would open up position and black would already have a huge advantage. Qe2 actualy offers black to exchange on e4, but that would open possibilites for check on b5. blacks e pawn still blocks LSB and white would have an advantage.
Whites LSB will go to g2 eventually so Qe2 does not really block it whatsoever.

notes.text: Your b-pawn grabs space and keeps the options of a5 followed by Ba6, or a bishop on b7.
notes.original:
I love to play b5 here. I am grabbing even more space with this move, also I will be able to finachheto my LSB on b7 and I leave possibility for a5 and Ba6 combination. Bishop fianchheto is a good option if there is still dynamics in the center of the board. Closing the center, Bb7 loses its credibility.
White has quit a few options here.
The most popular are :
# Re1 : Prepares kings side attack with Nf1--> h4-->Nfh2-->Ng4.
# a4 : Tries to block queenside pawn storm for some time. a4 blocks a5 in the future and forces black to play b4. After he stops queenside expansion, then white can start preparing Re1 and kingside attack. So this will be our main line.

notes.text: Keeping the bishop on c8 longer is sometimes better; decide between a5 with Ba6, or Bb7 right away.
notes.original: Somtimes it is better to keep bishop on c8 for longer. It is prudent to decide wheter to play a5 and then Ba6 or to go straight with Bb7.

notes.text: You are slightly better.
Your d-pawn stakes the centre in true French style, the most common choice here.
notes.original:
2...d5 continues to play in the style of the French defence. This is played most often, since most players playing e6 will be most comfortable with the French defence.

Black continues playing in the spirit of the French defence. White has a handful of options in this position, some better than others.

notes.text: Your c-pawn steers the game into the French Sicilian, a Sicilian with ...e6.
notes.original: 2...c5 is Black's second most common option. This steers the game into a Sicilian defence with e6, also known as the "French Sicilian."

notes.text: White keeps developing pieces. You can answer with ...Nf6, or gain space by pushing ...d4 to kick the knights.
notes.original:
3.Nc3 enters the Two Knights variation where White continues developing pieces instead of pawns. Black has two responses: either kick White's knights around and grab a space advantage with 3...d4, or let White take over the centre after 3...Nf6 4.e5 Nfd7 in order to undermine it in a similar fashion to the advance variation.

This is a relatively rare sideline of the French defence, and for good reason. White's approach is not particularly ambitious, which gives Black a relatively smooth game. Black has two main responses.

3...Nf6 is the main line. This allows White to push 4.e5 and after 4...Nfd7 5.d4 c5 Black gets a fairly thematic French structure, while White's knights are in the way of the pawns. Similar positions can be reached from the Steinitz variation where White plays f4 instead of Nf3, or the Advance variation where White can keep their centre together with c3.

3...d4 is Black's main alternative. This results in more open positions because after 4.Ne2 c5 5.c3 White is able to break apart Black's centre. Black can't hold onto their pawn and should instead prioritize development with 5...Nf6 or 5...Nc6.

notes.text: White wanted this: it backs up e5 and leaves you a weak d-pawn.
notes.original:
This is exactly what was white planning all along. He wants to fortify e5 pawn there and give black his weak d pawn to exchange. Black gets good development, better than in most french like defenses, but white will have many tricky ideas.
Main line here is Nc6. with pressuring e5 pawn. The other one is Bxc5.

notes.text: The fight is over e5; use the f and c files, and watch the diagonal toward f2.
notes.original: e5 square is the square white will be fighting for. Black needs to find ways over f file or c file. Also b6-f2 diagonal can give many great tactical ideas.

notes.text: You take the centre pawn, and it hits White's bishop, which must recapture.
Your knight develops by hitting White's loose bishop, which has to move again.
Your c-pawn strikes at White's last centre pawn, backed by your queen.
Your knight keeps the pressure on d4; taking on c5 or c6 would help you, not White.
notes.original:
Black is keeping pressure on d pawn.
1.) dxc5 ; Is really bad. It exchanges queens and gives bishop pair the power they need.
2.) Bxc6 is also bad. Seemingly weak doubled c pawns are actually hidden monsters which will completely destroy whites center, including the Ba6 possibility.

notes.text: You swap off White's last centre pawn, leaving it none in the middle.
Your knight eyes White's bishop on f3, ready to trade it off for the bishop pair.
Your bishop clears f8 so you can castle next and tuck your king away.
You take White's bishop with check, keeping both of yours against its one.
Your last minor piece gets out, covering c6 and clearing c8 for your rook.
You trade queens with check, so White's king must recapture and can no longer castle.
You win the pawn back, and your bishop hits the unguarded f2 pawn.
Trading bishops forces White to recapture with the f-pawn, leaving a lonely pawn on e3.
Your knight takes a central post, hitting the bishop and eyeing c4 and g4 near e3.
You win the piece back, keeping both bishops and opening the b-file for your rook.
Your bishop takes the open diagonal and pins the knight to White's rook.
Your queen backs up the c5 pawn and eyes b2 down the half-open file.
Your c-pawn takes control of d4 and lets your knight develop without blocking it.
notes.original:
The main move in this position is 3...c5, taking control over the d4-square. This is usually a useful move in the French defence. Making it sooner rather than later allows Black to develop their queenside knight without blocking the c-pawn. Because this move is so common, White is likely to be familiar with the resulting positions, so Black can try to deviate by playing a different move instead:

This is Black's most natural and common move.

4.c3 is not an effective way to get into the advance variation, since Black can play the move 4...d4, resulting in completely different positions.

notes.text: This is the Wing Gambit: White gives a b-pawn to clear your central pawns and build a full center.
notes.original:
This is the move which defines wing gambit. It is simmilar to Sicilian wing gambit as well. White waits to remove blacks central pawns in order to make his own full center, which is often hard to breach.
Wing Gambit in French Defense is very strong. White sacrifices b pawn and then plays a3. Plan is to exchange DSBs and to get Nb5-Nd6 move. Black can defend, but black will lack development for the most part of the opening. If black manages to defend, black has pretty much easy win with pawn up and better pawn structure.

notes.text: This transposes into the Nimzowitsch system of the Advance French.
notes.original: 4.d4 transposes into the Nimzowitsch system of the French advance variation.

notes.text: Accepting the gambit is the most principled reply; White will usually follow with a3 to open lines.
notes.original:
4...cxb4, accepting the gambit, is the most principled move. White is usually quick to offer the a-pawn as well, but this sacrifice is less likely to be accepted by Black.

White usually continues with the immediate 5.a3, hoping for Black to take the pawn and allowing White some open lines. However, Black doesn't have to take and can simply develop with 5...Nc6 with the idea to recapture on b4 with the dark-squared bishop. This does help White by letting them build up their centre with tempo, so after 6.axb4 Bxb4 7.c3 Be7 8.d4 White gets a space advantage in the centre in exchange for a pawn and allowing Black a passed pawn on the a-file.

Black can choose to take back the a3-pawn too with 5...bxa3. White can simply continue with 6.d4 to build up the centre and delay taking the pawn for now.

White doesn't have to offer up the a3 pawn immediately, they can simply build up the centre with 5.d4. These lines are likely to transpose back into lines with 5.a3.

notes.text: Another pawn is on offer; take it on a3.
notes.original: Yum! More pawns to eat!

notes.text: Your knight develops and hits the e5 pawn, leaving your bishop ready to retake on b4.
Your bishop takes back, keeping an extra pawn and pinning White's d-pawn to its king.
Your attacked bishop steps back to safety, where it also covers the g5 square.
Rb8 is critical; next a6 stops White's Nb5 ideas and covers the weak d6 square.
notes.original: This is critical move for black. Other variations such as Nh6, h5 or Bd7 leads to whites high development advantage. After Rb8, a6 is possible and it stops many breaches over weak d6 square via Nb5.

notes.text: Your a-pawn guards b5, so White's knight can't jump there on its way to d6.
Your b-pawn grabs queenside space and covers c4 against White's c-pawn and bishop.
Your h-pawn covers g4, so White's g-pawn can't chase a knight heading for f5.
Here you are fine with good counterplay, but you must remember the key Rb8 and h5 moves.
notes.original:
This is the position where blacks feels ok and has good counterplay. Before that, each move and each lost tempo losses the game.
Black has to remember few critical points, such as Rb8 and h5 moves.

notes.text: Taking on a3 lets White swap dark bishops, and Nb5 can't be stopped because a pawn is pinned.
notes.original: I dont recommend playing bxa3 as white will exchange DSBs. Nb5 is unstopable now, as a6 does not stop it because white rook is pinning a pawn.

notes.text: White's center is harder to attack, but you are up material; play carefully.
notes.original: We can't attack white's center as easily, but we are up material! This is a tricky line, so be careful, but if you are, you should be fine.

notes.text: Your pawn pushes on to stop White playing d4 and building a pawn centre.
Your knight backs up the d4 pawn and attacks White's e5 pawn.
Your knight develops, guards your extra b4 pawn and presses White's d4 pawn.
Your d-pawn hits the bishop on c4 and challenges White's centre.
notes.original:
2.Bc4 this move is playable but allows black to play 2...d5 and challenge the white center

One of the main drawbacks of playing 2.Bc4 in the French. D5 move attacks the Bc4.

notes.text: Your pawn takes its share of the centre, covering the c4 and e4 squares.
You win the pawn back and your bishop lands on a diagonal pointing at White's kingside.
Your knight comes out to watch the centre and clears the way to castle.
Your king gets tucked away before the centre opens, and your rook joins the game.
You win the pawn back and open the long diagonal for your light bishop.
Your queen and knight both hit the e5 pawn; the c5 pawn comes later once your bishop is free.
notes.original: We focus on capturing white's central pawn first. We can the target later his c pawn once our dark square bishop is unblocked.

notes.text: White's dark-square bishop is gone, so its pawns on dark squares are the targets.
notes.original: Majority of white's pawns are in the dark square. You can take advantage of the missing black dark square bishop.

notes.text: You trade on d4 to open the c-file and fix a White pawn there as a target.
The free pawn on d4 is a trap: taking it lets White win your queen.
notes.original: "Free pawn" trap

notes.text: Your knight trick won a pawn, and your bishop now attacks White's bishop on b5.
notes.original: [EXTRA] The knight trick! You won a pawn!

notes.text: Your knight on e7 can block checks, and you keep the plan of castling long and storming the kingside.
notes.original: We use the knight to block checks. We go with our plan of castling queen side and doing a pawn storm on the king side.

notes.text: Play your knight to d7 first, before ...Nf6, to avoid future tactics.
notes.original: Black must pay Knight to D7 first before playing Knight to F6 to avoid any future tatctics

notes.text: Main line: White takes your knight with check, and you recapture with the g-pawn.
notes.original: Main Line

notes.text: A side line: White retreats the knight to g3 instead of trading on f6.
notes.original: Side Line 1

notes.text: Another side line: White develops the bishop to g5 instead of trading on f6.
notes.original: Side Line 2

notes.text: You plan to castle long and attack on the kingside; the open g-file helps your rook.
notes.original: Idea is castle queen side and do a king side attack. The black h pawn is disposable as this opens another file for the rook.

notes.text: This quiet move makes no direct threat, so you can develop freely, but watch White's plan.
notes.original:
Another alternative but doesn't really give black that much of a problem
since this doesn't have a direct threat on the opening. Black is free to
play Nf6 b6 Bb7 Qd7 O-O-O But be wary of your opponent's plan.

notes.text: White aims for the Kasparov Attack setup: bishops to d3 and f4, knight to f3, then castling.
notes.original:
Kasparov Attack, although hasn't been named it is heavily associated with
the idea of Bd3 Bf4 Nf3 O-O.

notes.text: Trapy lines start here; your e5 break is the way to test White's setup.
notes.original: Trapy lines

notes.text: Your pawn attacks the bishop on b5, forcing White to decide what to do with it.
notes.original: Make sure to trade black's light square bishop

notes.text: Trapy line one: White takes on e5, and you can trade queens with check.
notes.original: Trapy Line 1

notes.text: Trapy line two: White develops the bishop, and you answer with the c-pawn push.
notes.original: Trapy Line 2

notes.text: This is one of the trappy lines, so stay alert to White's tricks here.
notes.original: Trapy Line 3

notes.text: Your queen checks on d3 and the king has no escape: checkmate.
notes.original: Checkmate!

notes.text: Your d7 knight guards f6, while White develops and keeps pressing that knight.
notes.original:
Protecting the knight, immune to tactics and vulnerability. White is
going to play something like Nf3 Bd3 c3 and of course short castle. White
would mantain the pressure on the knight (The f6 knight).

notes.text: Bg5 is easy to meet: just take the e4 pawn and keep developing.
notes.original:
Other variation such as Bg5 is quite easy to play. Black should just
simply take the pawn and continue with his opening principal and that is
developing.

notes.text: Your c-pawn hits the d4 pawn, White's last pawn in the center.
Your knight jumps into the center at once, hitting the c3 knight and challenging White's center.
notes.original:
Ne4! Why Ne4? Unlike the move Ne7! And follow up with c5! And so on,
black wants an immediate entry on the center. Beforehand black often tries
to breakup white's center since the move Ne7 is the usual move order. Now white is the one who's going to fight for black's center since black's
pawn would most likely be stuck there on e4!

notes.text: This is the usual Steinitz setup, but it needs lots of theory and leaves you a bit cramped.
notes.original:
This is the usual Steinitz System, but with this system, it's going to
take a lot of bloody theory plus extra homework. It also makes black's
position a little cramped.

notes.text: White's e5 blocked the center and gained a tempo on your knight, so both sides keep fighting for the center.
notes.original:
Lets talk about the Steinitz Variation with the Nd7 move order shall we?
Both players engage a fight for the center. Tension will increase even more
after Bg5 unless White wants to directly block the pawn structure and win a tempo by attacking the newly developed knight with e5.

notes.text: White threatens f3 against your e4 knight, but ...f6 challenges the center right away.
notes.original:
White wants to keep his knight because this plays an important role on
the center, which is why he is going to preserve it. On the other hand
black's knight is kinda misplaced on e4, biggest threat here is f3! But not to worry! Pawn to f6! Challenges white's center right away!

notes.text: Your a-pawn stops any White piece from landing on b5.
notes.original: Prevents any nasty threat of any piece landing on the b5 square.

notes.text: You plan to fianchetto your bishop on b7 so the e4 pawn stays fixed.
notes.original:
With idea of fianchettoing the bishop on b2 so that the pawn on e4 would
have been fixated in there.

notes.text: Your bishop on b7 backs up the e4 pawn, which stays fixed in place.
notes.original: Pawn is fixated!

notes.text: The f4 pawn holds up White's e5 pawn; your play will come on the queenside, starting with c5.
notes.original:
Pawn to f4 is the main move order in here, white wants to maintain his
central pawn just in case of uncertainty. Black in here should be aiming
for the queenside since this is the part where black's play would often derive from.

notes.text: A sideline that lets you play c5; it simply comes a move later than after f4.
notes.original:
Sideline, allows the move c5! Comes in delay with f4 but it is quite
possible.

notes.text: Your c-pawn challenges White's center; you attack on the queenside while White attacks on the kingside.
notes.original:
Challenging white's center right away! Black would then attack on the
queenside and white would attack on the kingside!

notes.text: Another way for White to keep the center together, with the knight guarding d4.
notes.original: Another alternative, trying to maintain the center of course.

notes.text: Keep aiming at the queenside, because that is where your play usually comes from.
notes.original:
Black in here should be aiming for the queenside since this is the part
where black's play would often derive from.

notes.text: White's a3 pawn takes b4 away from your c6 knight.
notes.original: Disallows Nb4 just in case.

notes.text: You attack on the queenside, and White's king is stuck in the center and hard to castle.
notes.original:
Black is attacking on the queenside, it would be quite a challenge for
white to dislodge this. White's king is still stuck on the center and he
would have a difficult time castling since white's kingside is weak and the queenside is under attacked!

notes.text: White's g3 may prepare play on the queenside, so stay alert there.
notes.original:
Dislodges Rg8, potentially dangerous since white would aim on the
queenside now.

notes.text: Your bishop pins the f3 knight, a key defender of d4, so you can undermine White's center.
notes.original: Trying to dislodge the d4 square.

notes.text: Castling long leaves you with a fine, flexible position.
notes.original: With a fine and flexible position for black!

notes.text: White has a slight lead in development, but cannot stop you from developing quickly.
notes.original:
White have a slight edge due to his piece development, but all I can say
is white cannot do anything in stopping black from developing in a haste.

notes.text: Castling long gives you a fine, flexible position.
notes.original: With a fine and flexible position for black!

notes.text: Castling long gives you a fine, flexible position.
notes.original: With a fine and flexible position for black!

notes.text: With no pawn on c3, you can retake with the queen and tempt White into a trap.
notes.original: Only now and if there is no pawn on C3 can Black take with the Queen amd temp White into a trap..

notes.text: If White tries to trap your queen with Bg5, you have a counter blow.
notes.original: IF Whites responds with Bishop to G5 attemting to trap thw Queen Black has a counter blow

notes.original: Bishop takes F3

notes.original: Only if the pawn is undefended will this tactic work

notes.text: White has doubled pawns and a weak kingside, while you are comfortable.
notes.original: White now has doubled pawns a weak kingside and Black is comfortable.

notes.original: If Whites goes for the sidestep simple sidestep with the King and dont take back to avoid any bishop check tactics losing Blacks Queen.

notes.text: This is White's second most popular way to play the position.
notes.original: This is white's second most popular way to play in the position.

notes.text: Developing the knight to f3 is White's main reply here.
